source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen by the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the philosophy according to the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. For Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken about them in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Now Apion the grammarian, who was called Plistonicus, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he was disposed in a rather hostile manner towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and having even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, the king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king in the place of Argive Inachus, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now this Ptolemaeus was a priest, and having set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, he says that under Amosis, the king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles; and of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger; and the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine generations younger, and this one is also said to be autochthonous. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are two generations younger. Now, going back to the time of the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the things of the Assyrians are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian rule, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the movement of Moses out of Egypt, under Amosis the Egyptian and under Inachus the Argive, occurred. And in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who was after Inachus, there was the flood that occurred during the time of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete.
pass_b_english: We will take up the question of how the philosophers' doctrines were observed by the Hebrews a little later, but first, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses. Through those times it will be shown beyond doubt that the philosophy of the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless the present memoir requires that we too run through what has been said on the subject. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian History*—though he writes with marked hostility toward the Hebrews, being himself an Egyptian by birth and the author of a treatise against the Jews—mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemy of Mendes as his witness. Ptolemy's words are these: "Amosis, having become king in the time of the Argive Inachus, dug up Avaris," as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest who set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, and he states that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses. From this it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus. The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argolic, which begin with Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Of these, the Attic line that springs from Cecrops—who was two-natured and autochthonous, to use Tatian's exact words—is forty generations younger; the Arcadian line from Pelasgus is nine generations younger, and Pelasgus himself is also said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic line from Deucalion is two generations younger than the Arcadian. Reckoning from Inachus down to the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted, amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years. But if the Assyrian records are far older than the Greek, as Ctesias asserts, then the exodus of Moses from Egypt under the Egyptian Amosis and the Argive Inachus falls in the 402nd year of the Assyrian empire and the 32nd year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who succeeded Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus, the kingdom in Sicyon—first under Aegialeus, then Eurypus, then Telchin—and the kingdom of Crete in Crete.
